newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND HAS NEW CONSTIUTION - OFFICIAL POLL RESULTS.
newsitem.headline: POLAND HAS NEW CONSTIUTION - OFFICIAL POLL RESULTS.

text.p: In a nationwide referendum on Sunday Poles narrowly approved a new constitution, which replaces the old, communist-era charter, official results of the referendum released late on Monday showed.

PAP news agency quoted the State Election Commission as saying that out of those taking part in the polls 52.71 percent backed the new constitution while 45.89 percent were opposed, with 1.40 percent of votes invalid. Out of 28.32 million of eligible voters, 42.86 percent cast their vote.

The constitution, designed to enshrine Poland's democratic transformation since the 1989 fall of communism, was drafted by the ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and its Peasant allies together with two opposition parties in parliament.
It was passed by parliament on April 2 and will take effect in just over three months.
A "no" verdict would have left Poland with remains of its discredited 1952 Stalinist constitution, amended by 1992 interim laws, until some future parliament could agree on a new version.
The constitution broadly retains the current political system while weakening the presidency. It sets caps on the government's spending but obliges it to support employment and home building.

The constitution was strongly criticised by the Solidarity Electoral Action (AWS) -- a group of some 30 small right-wing parties clustered round the Solidarity trade union -- which hopes to win power after the September parliamentary polls.

The AWS, seeing Poland's history as bound up with the majority Roman Catholic faith, had wanted the charter to clearly invoke God, put religious values above man-made law and include a clause effectively banning abortion -- now legal in Poland.
The bishops, concerned over abortion, had voiced deep moral reservations about the document.
The right also said a section allowing Poland to surrender by treaty some functions to international organisations -- to ease entry into European structures -- limited sovereignty.
The constitution's authors rejected these arguments as false.
They said their version made room for people of all faiths or none and, for example, left open the possibility of changing the abortion law by a future majority in parliament.
